entry.title: Keep the gloss model loaded between lookups
entry.content:
Keep the gloss model loaded between lookups

Warming the model at startup only helps the first word. Ollama unloads an
idle model after 5 minutes, which is shorter than the gaps between lookups
when you're reading a page and then picking a word out of it — so the model
drops out mid-session and the next word pays the load cost all over again.

Send keep_alive with every request, defaulting to 30 minutes. It goes on
every request rather than just the warm-up because Ollama restarts the
unload timer from whatever value it saw last: a Define without it would
silently put the model back on the 5-minute default.

The right value depends on the machine — a large base model on a laptop is
worth unloading promptly, on a workstation worth keeping resident — so it's
configurable via --ollama-keep-alive and ollama_keep_alive. The value is
validated at startup, before the Ollama round-trip: it rides on every
lookup, so a typo Ollama rejects would otherwise fail every word once the
review screen is already open.

entry.title: Warm the gloss model at startup
entry.content:
Warm the gloss model at startup

Loading the model costs seconds — more since the base model became Qwen —
and left alone that cost lands on the first word the user picks, after the
review screen is already open, where the wait is most visible.

Fire a throwaway lookup in a goroutine as soon as the provider is built, so
the load overlaps the setup still to come (fetching the source, building the
document, starting the TUI) and the reading the user does before picking
anything.

It sends a real lookup rather than a bare load request: that makes Ollama
evaluate the Modelfile's system prompt and its ~40 few-shot examples as well
as loading the weights, and both are reused by the lookups that follow.
Nothing waits on the result — a warm-up that fails costs nothing, because
the same failure recurs on the first genuine lookup, which reports it
properly.

entry.title: Move by screen row, not document line
entry.content:
Move by screen row, not document line

j/k jumped to the first word of the next document line, so on a zoomed-in
terminal — where one sentence wraps over most of the screen — a single
press skipped everything in between. The render now reports the row and
column each word wrapped onto, and j/k walk those rows, keeping the
cursor's column like vim's gj/gk. Scrolling centers on the cursor's own
row too, rather than on the row its line began at.

entry.title: install takes no flags; both inputs are config
entry.content:
install takes no flags; both inputs are config

A --base-model flag isn't merely redundant with the config key, it's
incoherent. install's output is the durable artifact, so there's no "just
this once" for it: a base passed on the command line stays installed until
the next `ankix install` — which every upgrade now asks you to run — puts
the default back without saying so. That's the exact durability trap the
checksum pinning was added to close, and nothing else reads the value, so
config is the only place the choice can survive.

install now defines no flags at all. The name it builds is the global
--ollama-model, the same one every command looks up; the base model is
`base_model`. A test walks its flag set to keep it that way.

entry.title: One flag for the model name, not two
entry.content:
One flag for the model name, not two

`ankix install --model` and the global `--ollama-model` named the same
thing: the model install builds is exactly the model every other command
looks up. Two ways to say it is two ways to disagree — which it already did,
before the previous commit made both read the same config key.

Drop the install-only flag. `--ollama-model` (config `ollama_model`) is now
the single name, and a test asserts install doesn't reintroduce one of its
own. Breaking for anyone scripting `ankix install --model`, which is nobody.

While auditing for the same duplication elsewhere: the README documented a
`--model` flag on `kindle vocab` that has never existed, and omitted
`--limit` and `--headless`, which do. mise's create task now takes MODEL
alongside BASE_MODEL rather than hardcoding the name.

entry.title: Make the base model and model name durable config
entry.content:
Make the base model and model name durable config

Pinning the model to the Modelfile checksum means every upgrade asks for a
rebuild — which turned --base-model into the same durability bug the pinning
was meant to fix. Build on qwen2.5:14b once, upgrade, run the `ankix install`
the error tells you to, and you're silently back on llama3.2:3b.

base_model belongs in the config file, alongside every other setting that's
a property of the install rather than of one invocation. --base-model still
overrides it for a single run.

The same class of bug was already there between the two model-name flags:
`ankix install --model` hardcoded "ankix" while every other command read
ollama_model from config, so setting that key built one model and looked up
another, and the lookup failed with "no ankix-es model installed" naming a
model install had never been asked to build. Both now default from the same
key.

entry.title: Pin the Ollama model to the Modelfile's checksum
entry.content:
Pin the Ollama model to the Modelfile's checksum

ankix's prompt lives in the Ollama model, not the binary, so the two have to
agree — a release with new prompt rules is useless against a model an older
release built. Until now nothing noticed: the refine feature's Correction:
turn was simply answered as if it were a new word to translate, and the only
mitigation was a README note asking people to remember `ankix install`.

Rather than detect staleness after the fact, bind the two by name. `ankix
install` now tags the model with a short checksum of the Modelfile it was
built from, and every command asks for exactly that tag. A model built by an
older release isn't stale so much as unaddressable — nothing has to compare
versions, because the wrong model can't be reached in the first place.

The checksum covers the Modelfile as committed, deliberately not the
rendered output: the FROM line is the one part that varies per install, and
a command resolving a model at runtime has no idea which base model was
used. So the tag names the prompt, and --base-model stays an orthogonal
choice.

A missing model is now reported before any slow setup work rather than as a
per-word "lookup failed" once the review screen is already open, so the
provider is built up front — which also collapses four copies of the
--no-gloss branch into one helper. The three cases read differently and say
different things: an upgrade that left an older build behind names both tags
and the command that fixes it, a first run says to install, and a model
named explicitly with --ollama-model isn't something `ankix install` can
fix, so it doesn't suggest it.

A name with an explicit tag is used verbatim, which is the escape hatch for
a hand-built or forked model, and old builds are kept rather than deleted:
they share their weights, and an older binary keeps working against the tag
it expects.

Cobra printed the full flag list under these errors, burying the fix.
Silencing usage from PersistentPreRunE rather than on the command means it
only applies once args have validated, so a genuine usage error still gets
usage. SilenceErrors makes main the single place errors are printed.

ollama/vocab/mise.toml's create task computes the same tag in shell; a test
checks the two agree, since a mismatch would build a model nothing can find.

Let the user correct a translation by prompting the model

entry.title: Let the user correct a translation by prompting the model
entry.content:
Let the user correct a translation by prompting the model

Small local models drift: a translation comes back with a neighboring
adjective attached ("new keys" for "llaves"), or takes the literal sense of
a word the sentence uses figuratively. Re-scoping the phrase doesn't help —
the phrase was right, the answer was wrong — so the only recourse was
deleting the word and losing the card.

Press r on a marked word in any review screen, type what's wrong in plain
language, and the correction goes to the model as a follow-up turn on its
own answer. Corrections chain off the current value, so a couple of passes
can narrow in.

dict.Refiner is a separate, optional interface: a provider with nothing to
re-ask (a plain dictionary lookup) simply doesn't implement it, and the key
is inert when the assertion fails — which also covers --no-gloss, where the
Provider is nil.

Two ways a refinement could be silently thrown away, both fixed here:

  - An ordinary lookup already in flight for the same phrase would land on
    top of it. Phrase text can't tell the two apart, because refining
    doesn't change the text, so lookups are now tagged with a monotonic
    generation instead. That also fixes a pre-existing bug where Kindle,
    which rebuilds its phrases between sentence groups, could apply one
    group's result to the next group's phrase.
  - Cancelling an expansion reverts lo/hi but not previewText, so the
    follow-up refresh re-fetched a plain gloss over the correction.
    Refinements are sticky now, and cleared only when the phrase's own
    bounds actually move.

A failed refine keeps the answer it was asked to correct, rather than
leaving the user with nothing.

Kindle quit on a bare q before dispatching by state; typing "quitar" into a
correction would have quit mid-review and lost the sentence group. The
refine prompt joins the sentence editor in that exclusion, and handles
ctrl+c itself since textinput doesn't.

Modelfile: rules 12 and 13 define the "Correction:" turn — it revises the
previous answer, outranks the don't-include-neighboring-words rules when
asked to, and a correction about form ("shorter") must not become part of
the answer. num_predict 24 -> 48 so a correction can't truncate the reply
before the "|", and num_ctx 4096 -> 8192.

Only one correction few-shot, on a sentence used nowhere else. Measured
against the existing 48-case eval: three correction examples cost 5 cases,
mostly because they reused sentences that already had plain examples and
taught two answers for the same input. One example on a fresh sentence
costs nothing (39/48, same as before) and still passes all 6 correction
cases off the prose rules alone.

Requires a one-time `ankix install` rebuild; an older model answers
"Correction: shorter" as if it were a new word, which ankix can't detect,
so the parse error now suggests the rebuild.

Closes #8
